div.p: This paper represents one of few attempts to address the issue of low power design for real-time systems. We present a power reduction method at the software compilation level. Given a real-time program, an interinstruction power reduction technique is proposed to transform the program to another one with lower power consumption. In addition, a scheduling algorithm for realtime operating systems is proposed [I] to reschedule realtime programs when the execution time of the programs is changed. Therefore, the proposed scheduling algorithm works together with the proposed power reduction technique to make sure all programs meet their deadlines and to improve the system schedulability. We also evaluate the performance of the proposed inter-instruction reduction method by comparing it with the cold scheduling algorithm and show that the proposed method outperforms the cold scheduling algorithm and reduces more energy power.

div.head: Introduction
div.p: Real-time Systems are characterized by the requirements of functional correctness as well as temporal correctness. Late execution is considered as failure in realtime systems and may result in catastrophes. Applications in real-time systems have often been modeled as periodic tasks monitoring sensors and responding to the changes in the environment repeatedly. For examples, air defense systems require prompt response to the intrusion of unknown missiles; nuclear power plants need timely actions on sudden temperature change in the reactors; and industry product lines shall remove defect products in the production lines immediately. Therefore, periodic tasks play an important role in the design and the implementation of real-time systems.

Most real-time systems use embedded systems as an execution platform. One outstanding feature of embedded systems is the strong coupling between hardware and software components. The hardware of embedded systems is application-oriented while the software is application-specific program running on a dedicated hardware. Embedded system are often located in the special environment (such as stand-alone or isolated environment) where power consumption is a big concern. Upon the presence of power restriction and real-time constraints, low power design has significant impact on the performance and the schedulability of real-time systems: Energy saving. Consider the periodic execution of real-time programs. We apply power reduction techniques on periodic programs in advance and obtain new version of the programs with lower power consumption. Since the programs are executed repeatedly, low power design for periodic programs saves more energy in the overall power consumption than that for sporadic programs which are only executed once. 0 Execution time. Power reduction techniques can be applied to a chipset, an instruction set, or program codes. A chipset with lower power consumption consists of fewer transistors and hence executes faster. Same theory applies to program codes. A sequence of instructions in a program may be replaced by a complex instruction which consumes less power. Therefore, power reduction techniques change the execution time of a program. Schedulability. Execution time represents one of the main characteristics of real-time programs and has strong impact on the system schedulability. For a given deadline constraint, it is easier for a program with short execution time to meet the deadline. Power reduction changes the power consumption as well as the execution time of a program. Therefore, it changes the system schedulability.

There is a hierarchy for the low power design ranging from the semi-conductor level, the logic gate level, the chipset architecture level, the operating system level, up to the software compilation level. Several power reduction techniques are proposed at the three low levels of the hierarchy (semi-conductor, logic gate, and chipset levels) [3]. In this paper, we consider the low power design issue for real-time systems at the operating system and software compilation levels.

div.head: Instruction Level Power Estimation
div.p: The estimation of the power consumption by a program is based on the compiled instruction sequence. The instruction level power model has been proposed [6] and the estimated energy cost for a program can be formalized as follows. where Ep denotes the energy cost of a program p ; Bj denotes the base cost of an instruction i; Nj represents the number of times instruction i is executed; Oi,j represents the inter-instruction cost between two consecutive instructions i andj; Nj,j is the number of times such two consecutive instructions are executed; Ek represents the run-time energy overhead for each cache miss or pipeline stall. The energy cost consumed by program p , Ep, consists of three energy costs: the base costs of all instructions in the program, the inter-instruction cost of each consecutive instruction pair, and the run-time energy overhead. The goal of the paper is to develop the power reduction technique for real-time programs, given that these values are known a prior.

Note that the power estimation at the instruction level described in equation 1 does not take context switching into account. Consider a case in which a program is preempted many times and another case that the program is executed alone in a system. The circuit states for these two cases are totally different. The former case is more complicated and induces more overhead than the other. Consequently, the calculation of the inter-instruction costs (Ol,,'s) does not count for the real inter-instruction effect in run time. In order to guarantee the timing constraints, the system should restricts the depth of preemption to reduce the overhead induced by context switching. Uncontrolled context switching contradicts a bounded execution time and thus prevents any possibility for guarantee. Program execution should avoid context switching to get a closer estimated value on the power consumption.

div.head: Real-Time System Model
div.p: Our real-time system model consists of a set of periodic real-time programs. Let the Elemental Unit (EU) [4] be the smallest non-preemptable execution unit which is triggered by incoming data and signals, operates on the data, and produces output data and signals. The execution of an EU is atomic and the resources needed by an EU are ready before its execution and will be hold for the entire execution. Each program can be described by an elemental unit graph (EUG), where an EUG is a directed acyclic graph (DAG); each node is an EU; and each directed edge represents the precedence and communication relationships between EUs. The timing constraints for a program are imposed on the boundary of EUs of the program.

The power estimation shown in equation 1 can be applied to each EU. Since all EUs are non-preemptable, the inter-instruction cost is correctly measured by O,,'s. Given an EU which consists of a sequence of instructions, we assume that the execution time can be estimated and hence is known a priori.

div.head: Relative Timing Model
div.p: Real-time systeins have been traditionally using the absolute timing model to specify the temporal requirements. The absolute timing model uses deadline, start time, and period to describe timing constraints. Such timing constraints impose a fixed time interval during which an EU can be executed. Neither inter-EU dependencies nor temporal relationships between two instances of a periodic EU can be specified.

The relative timing model is more flexible on describing the relative temporal dependency between two EUs. It specifies the temporal requirements in terms of the offsets from the periods, the relative timing constraints are usually imposed on the start time and the finish time of EUs. For example, 1. The consecutive executions of the instances of EU, are separated at least 5 ms and at most 10 ms.
2. The start time of EU, is no later than 8 ms after EU, completes.

In the literature, relative timing constraints on contemporary real-time applications have been adopted and studied [ 2 ] . In this paper, the proposed real-time scheduling algorithm adapts the relative timing model and generates a calendar which satisfies all the timing constraints. A calendar specifies the start time and finish time of all EUs.

div.head: The Real-Tiime Scheduling Problem with PowerConsumption Minimization
div.p: The input to the real-time scheduling problem includes (1) a sequence of compiled EUs (from the realtime programs in a real-time system), (2) relative timing constraints imposed on the EUs, (3) energy consumption values for all the instructions and all the pairs of instructions in the instruction set. A sequence of compiled EUs is obtained from the compiler and the timing analyzer of a real-time system. The resource requirements and the synchronization constraints are extracted from the system specification. The synchronization and the semantic constraints (such as precedence, mutual exclusion, etc.) determine the execution order of EUs.
The input is formalized as follows.

A sequence of EUs, ( p i , p2, ..., pn}. The execution of EUpi is followed by that of EUpi+l. si and fi denote the start time and the finish time of an EUpi, respectively. Since each EU is non-preemptable, it implies that fi 5 si+], V i . The execution time of EUpi, , V i is known apriori.(For a given sequence of instructions, we can calculate the execution time of that sequence of instructions.) The base energy values for an instruction i, Bi, b' i, and the inter-instruction cost for a pair of instructions i and j , Oi,j, V i, j, are given as a prior information.

The considered scheduling problem is to schedule a given set of EUs, where the total energy consumption of EUs is the minimum, subject to a set of the relative timing constraints imposed on the EUs The timing constraints are specified by equation 2. The energy cost for each EU can be calculated by equation 1 and hence the total energy consumption for a set of EUs can be obtained accordingly. Such scheduling problem with the low power optimization is an NP-complete problem. Therefore, we propose a heuristic solution for the given problem.

div.head: The Proposed Scheduling Algorithm
div.p: As mentioned before, the execution time might be changed if the low-power reduction techniques are applied. The reduction is done off-line and hence we need an offline scheduling algorithm. The proposed scheduling algorithm works with the proposed interinstructionreduction algorithm described in Section 5 and generates a calendar which is used for executing the EUs.

In the calendar, the information about the start time and finish time of all power-reduced EUs is kept. The calendar can be used by the run-time scheduler and dispatcher in real-time operating systems [4].

The power reduction on an EU is accepted only if all EUs in the system are schedulable after the reduction. Hence, we need an algorithm to test if the change is acceptable or not. The proposed scheduling algorithm achieves three functions: (1) to generate an initial calendar, (2) to test if a change to the execution time of an EU is acceptable, and (3) to adjust a calendar dynamically when the execution time of an EU is changed.

The main idea of the scheduling algorithm can be described as follows. Initially, according to the set of relative timing constraint, TC, specified by equation 2, we can calculate the range of start time of EU,. The minimum value in this range is taken, that is, to start EU, as soon as possible. This value is denoted as SI'.

Since S,' is a determinate number, we can substitute this value for SI in all inequalities in TC. From S,' and the substituted inequalities which involve EU,, we can deduce a range for the execution time of EU,. The range is specified by an upper bound and a low bound. Given this interval of the execution time, we can apply low-power reduction technique to EU, to obtain an adjusted version of the elemental unit. The adjusted version should be acceptable only if the execution time of the adjusted version still falls into this range. We denote the adjusted execution time of EU, as e,'.

According to this determinate number e,', we can substitute this value for e, in all inequalities in TC. Deduce a new set of the timing constraint from the old set. Repeat the same procedure for next EU until all element units are processed. More details can be found in the work [l].

div.head: Inter-Instruction Power Reduction
div.p: The execution order of a sequence of instructions in an EU may be changed without changing the semantics and functionality of the EU. Changing the execution sequence of instructions can reduce the inter-instruction cost of power consumption. However, the execution order can not be altered randomly. The data dependency, precedence, and resource synchronization relationship shall be retained. A directed acyclic graph can be used to specify the relation between instructions in an EU. Such a graph is called the relationship graph (RG) of an EU.

Given the RG of an EU, all the possible combinations of instruction sequence can be generated by using topological sorting. Unfortunately, it is an NPcomplete problem to try out all the possible sequences and to find the optimal sequence with the minimum cost. Therefore, we propose a heuristic reduction algorithm to solve the problem.

For a given instruction sequence and the RG of an EU, the proposed reduction algorithm examines instructions one by one according to the initial instruction sequence. No matter how the algorithm changes the execution order, the constraints in the RG need to be satisfied -an instruction should be executed after all its predecessors in the RG are executed. Therefore, all the possible positions for an examined instruction can be any positions after the predecessors of the examined instruction. In each iteration of the algorithm, the sequence with the minimum cost is kept. If the changing of the position of the examined instruction reduces the total power consumption, a new sequence with less cost is found. The algorithm terminates when all instructions are examined. Since it takes O(n) to compute the total power consumption for a sequence of instruction, the algorithm requires time complexity of O(n3) to complete the reduction. div.head: Performance Evaluation
div.p: To evaluate the performance of the proposed algorithm, we write a program to simulate. We compare our algorithm with the cold scheduling algorithm which is proposed by Su et a1 [5]. The basic idea of the cold scheduling algorithm is to reduce the inter-instruction power consumption cost by changing the execution order of the instructions in a sequence. Given a sequence of n instructions, the cold scheduling algorithm starts, from the first position until the nth position, to find out the suitable instruction for each position. Denote the instruction assigned to position p as Ins,. The candidate instructions for position p are the ones that do not violate the precedence constraints between them and Insp-]. One of the candidate instructions for position p is chosen as Insp. In the cold scheduling algorithm, the instruction whose inter-instruction cost between it and Insp-l is the minimum is chosen a5 Inspp. We compare the performance of our algorithm with that of the cold scheduling algorithm. We define the reduction rate as the performance measurement: the reduced energy cost over the initial energy, where the reduced energy cost equals the initial cost minus the cost after the reduction algorithm is applied. Note that the total cost for the base energy for a sequence of instructions is identical for these inter-instruction reduction algorithms and is therefore ignored in the performance experiments. For each experiment (by fixing the above arguments), the program randomly generates 10,000 runs to simulate the two algorithms and compare them with the unreduced cases. The final energy cost of an experiment is the collected and averaged data over-1 0,000 runs. Table 1 plots tihe average power consumption for the experiments where NumInstSet = 128. Table 2 shows the reduction rates for the experiments where NumInstSet =128. In Table 2, we use the averaged initial cost (i.e. without applying any reduction algorithm) as a reference. The tables show that the proposed algorithm reduces more energy as the size of EU becomes larger. The X axis in these tables indicates the number of instructions in an EU (i.e. NumInstEU). When the value of NumInstEU is small, the number of possible combinations for the execution order is small and herice the reduction is limited. As the value of NumInstEU increases, our algorithm finds a better execution order which reduces more energy cost. It shows that our algorithm performs better than the cold scheduling algorithm dose. Table 3 plots the reduction rates of our algorithm for different sizes of instruction sets and uses the averaged initial cost as a reference. Possible sizes of instruction sets considered are 16, 32, 64, and 128. The X axis indicates the size of an EU. It shows that as the size of instruction set increases, the reduction rate increases accordingly.
